title: End-to-End Differentiable Diffusion Conditioning for Physics-Informed Optimization

paper.title: End-to-End Differentiable Diffusion Conditioning for Physics-Informed Optimization
paper.abstract:
Abstract Optimizing high-dimensional physical systems under expensive evaluations and
complex constraints is a central challenge in science and engineering. In
offline model-based optimization (MBO), methods must improve designs using only
a fixed dataset and no test-time access to the true objective. However,
existing methods typically suffer from conservatism, unconstrained surrogate
exploitation, or function as static inference-time samplers that cannot refine
candidates against precise physical objectives. In this paper, we propose Differentiable Diffusion
Conditioning (D2C) for offline MBO, which leverages the fact that deterministic sampling makes the reverse denoising
chain differentiable with respect to the conditioning signal. D2C turns a
frozen conditional diffusion model into an end-to-end gradient-based optimizer
by directly optimizing conditioning variables at test time via gradients from
frozen surrogate objectives and physics-informed penalties backpropagated
through the reverse chain. We implement this idea in
a composed proposer-evaluator framework and evaluate it on laser pulse
optimization for inertial confinement fusion, sustainable data-center workload
scheduling, and four Design-Bench tasks. Our method achieves the strongest
results on the two real-world tasks and the best average rank across four
Design-Bench tasks.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: The optimization of complex physical systems remains one of the most consequential challenges in science and engineering. Problems such as laser pulse shaping for inertial confinement fusion (ICF) and workload scheduling in large-scale data centers share a common structure: objective functions are computationally expensive to evaluate, the design space is high-dimensional with non-linear correlations, and candidate solutions must satisfy strict physical constraints where any violation carries safety-critical consequences. The offline model-based optimization (MBO) paradigm addresses the evaluation-cost bottleneck by learning entirely from a fixed dataset of previously evaluated designs, with no access to the true objective at test time. Within this paradigm, existing approaches fall into three broad families. Forward (surrogate-based) methods train a neural network to approximate the objective and perform gradient ascent in design space [ 31 , 9 ] ; while effective, optimizing directly in unconstrained design space can move into regions poorly supported by the offline data, where the surrogate is unreliable. Inverse methods learn a conditional mapping from target performance labels to designs [ 2 , 19 , 18 , 22 ] ; these tend to stay closer to the empirical data distribution but are limited by the performance ceiling of the training labels and struggle to extrapolate beyond observed optima. Trajectory-based methods construct synthetic improvement paths and train generative models to imitate optimization dynamics [ 3 , 39 ] ; while powerful, they remain inference-time samplers whose conditioning targets are fixed prior to generation, with no mechanism to refine designs against downstream objectives. A common limitation across these families is the lack of a direct, differentiable path from a physics-informed objective back to the generative process. The conditioning signal that steers generation is treated as a static input rather than an optimizable variable. This decoupling is especially limiting in safety-critical physical domains where the objective is not a single scalar score but a composite of performance metrics, conservation laws, and hard feasibility constraints that must be jointly satisfied. We address these limitations by proposing Differentiable Diffusion Conditioning (D2C) for Physics-Informed Optimization, a novel approach that converts a conditional diffusion model into an end-to-end gradient-based optimizer for constrained physical design. Our key insight for offline MBO is that deterministic diffusion sampling renders the reverse chain differentiable with respect to the conditioning input, enabling end-to-end backpropagation from downstream physics-informed objectives, through a frozen surrogate evaluator and physics-informed penalty terms, back to the conditioning variables. D2C therefore optimizes conditioning directly at test time while keeping both the diffusion proposer and surrogate evaluator fixed, yielding a practical end-to-end gradient path from the downstream objective to the conditioning variables. The diffusion model tends to keep candidates closer to the data distribution, while surrogate and physics-informed losses steer them toward feasible, high-performing designs. We embed this mechanism within a composed proposer-evaluator architecture: the diffusion model G θ G_{\theta} (proposer) generates candidates, and a surrogate S ϕ S_{\phi} (evaluator) scores them, with both remaining fixed during test-time optimization. Only the conditioning input is updated, which helps keep optimization closer to the proposer’s learned data distribution while limiting direct surrogate exploitation. A stochastic multi-objective weighting scheme and validity-first selection further encourage broad exploration of competing objective trade-offs while enforcing strict constraint satisfaction. Figure 1 provides an overview of the full D2C pipeline. Our main contributions are: • End-to-End Conditioning Optimization Through Diffusion. We use the deterministic reverse diffusion chain to backpropagate end-to-end from composite physics objectives to the conditioning inputs, making the conditioning signal itself the optimization variable within the generative process; optimizing it outperforms optimizing the latent noise (Appendix D.7 ). • Frozen Proposer-Evaluator Architecture. We introduce a composed proposer-evaluator architecture in which a frozen diffusion proposer helps keep candidates closer to the empirical data distribution, while a frozen surrogate evaluator provides optimization gradients, reducing out-of-distribution exploitation. • Physics-Informed Multi-Objective Optimization. We integrate heterogeneous objectives directly into the differentiable sampling chain via a stochastic Dirichlet-weighted loss, enabling principled multi-objective optimization under domain-specific constraints. • Strong Empirical Performance. D2C achieves the best results on the two real-world physical design tasks and the best average rank across four Design-Bench tasks. Figure 1: Overview of D2C. A frozen conditional diffusion proposer generates designs from conditioning inputs, a frozen surrogate evaluator and physics-informed penalties define a differentiable test-time objective, and gradients are backpropagated through the deterministic DDIM chain to optimize the conditioning signal. Multiple noise trials and loss-weight samples produce a candidate pool, from which the best valid design is selected after domain-specific constraint checks.

sections.heading: 2.2 Deterministic DDIM Sampling
sections.text: Denoising Diffusion Implicit Models (DDIM) [ 29 ] generalize the sampling process by considering a non-Markovian forward process that yields the same marginals as DDPM. Crucially, DDIM allows for a deterministic mapping from a latent noise x T x_{T} to a clean sample x 0 x_{0} . The update rule is given by: x t − 1 = α ¯ t − 1 ​ ( x t − 1 − α ¯ t ​ ϵ θ ​ ( x t , c , t ) α ¯ t ) + 1 − α ¯ t − 1 ​ ϵ θ ​ ( x t , c , t ) x_{t-1}=\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t-1}}\left(\frac{x_{t}-\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\epsilon_{\theta}(x_{t},c,t)}{\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t}}}\right)+\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t-1}}\epsilon_{\theta}(x_{t},c,t) (3) Eq. ( 3 ) gives the fully deterministic DDIM update ( σ t = 0 \sigma_{t}=0 ), in which the stochastic noise term is omitted and the sampling chain becomes a deterministic discrete mapping from x T x_{T} to x 0 x_{0} . This update can be viewed as a discrete analogue of the probability-flow ODE perspective, but here we rely only on the finite-step deterministic map induced by the sampler. This determinism ensures that the mapping G θ : ( c , x T ) ↦ x 0 G_{\theta}:(c,x_{T})\mapsto x_{0} is differentiable with respect to the conditioning input c c .

sections.heading: 2.3 Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG)
sections.text: Classifier-Free Guidance is a technique to improve the adherence of the generated samples to the conditioning signal c c . During training, the conditioning c c is randomly replaced with a null token ∅ \emptyset with probability p drop p_{\mathrm{drop}} . At inference time, the noise estimate is interpolated between the conditional and unconditional predictions: ϵ ~ θ ​ ( x t , c , t ) = ϵ θ ​ ( x t , ∅ , t ) + w ⁡ ( ϵ θ ​ ( x t , c , t ) − ϵ θ ​ ( x t , ∅ , t ) ) \tilde{\epsilon}_{\theta}(x_{t},c,t)=\epsilon_{\theta}(x_{t},\emptyset,t)+w(\epsilon_{\theta}(x_{t},c,t)-\epsilon_{\theta}(x_{t},\emptyset,t)) (4) where w ≥ 0 w\geq 0 is the guidance scale ( w = 0 w=0 yields unconditional sampling, w = 1 w=1 recovers standard conditional sampling, and w > 1 w>1 amplifies conditioning adherence). In D2C, we use this guidance not only to bias sampling but also to provide a stable optimization regime in which gradient-based updates of c c can proceed.

sections.heading: 3 Methodology
sections.text: We present Differentiable Diffusion Conditioning (D2C), a framework that enables a pretrained conditional diffusion model to function as an end-to-end gradient-based optimizer for physical design. The key idea is a composed proposer-evaluator architecture in which a conditional diffusion model serves as a differentiable proposer and a frozen forward surrogate provides a training-time consistency signal and inference-time gradient guidance. Algorithm 1 summarizes the full pipeline. We describe each component below.

The surrogate S ϕ S_{\phi} is trained independently on the same dataset and remains frozen throughout. This architecture serves two roles: providing a surrogate consistency signal during training (Section 3.3 ) and an objective gradient ∇ x 0 ℒ obj \nabla_{x_{0}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{obj}} during inference-time optimization (Section 3.5 ).

sections.heading: 3.5 Inference-Time Conditioning Optimization
sections.text: With G θ G_{\theta} and S ϕ S_{\phi} , we optimize c opt c_{\mathrm{opt}} by backpropagating a composite loss through the DDIM chain. The loss is a weighted combination of K K differentiable penalty terms: ℒ = ∑ k = 1 K λ k ​ ℒ k ​ ( x 0 , x ref , c fix ) , \mathcal{L}=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\lambda_{k}\,\mathcal{L}_{k}(x_{0},\,x_{\mathrm{ref}},\,c_{\mathrm{fix}}), (13) where each ℒ k \mathcal{L}_{k} is a scalar loss computed from the generated design x 0 = G θ ​ ( c , x T ) x_{0}=G_{\theta}(c,x_{T}) , the reference design x ref x_{\mathrm{ref}} , and/or the fixed conditioning c fix c_{\mathrm{fix}} (e.g., the surrogate evaluation S ϕ ​ ( x 0 , c fix ) S_{\phi}(x_{0},c_{\mathrm{fix}}) ), and the weights 𝝀 = ( λ 1 , … , λ K ) \boldsymbol{\lambda}=(\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{K}) control the trade-off among competing objectives. Crucially, no loss term depends directly on the optimizable component c opt c_{\mathrm{opt}} ; all losses are functions of the realized design x 0 x_{0} only. The loss terms are domain-specific but follow a common taxonomy. In practice, any first-order optimizer (e.g., Adam) can replace vanilla gradient descent; the key requirement is differentiability of the full chain. Crucially, only c opt c_{\mathrm{opt}} receives gradient updates; θ \theta and ϕ \phi remain frozen. This mitigates the risk of surrogate exploitation common in unconstrained model-based optimization [ 31 ] : under suitably tuned guidance, the generative model helps keep designs closer to the empirical data distribution induced by the learned prior while the surrogate provides only a directional gradient signal.

sections.heading: 4 Experiments
sections.text: We evaluate D2C on two sets of tasks: (i) two real-world physical design problems where constraint satisfaction is safety-critical, and (ii) the standard Design-Bench [ 30 ] benchmark suite for offline model-based optimization. Although D2C is motivated by constrained physical domains, we also evaluate it on Design-Bench to test whether the same mechanism remains strong on standard offline MBO benchmarks beyond the application domains that motivate the method. Additional implementation, hyperparameter, and evaluation details are provided in Appendices A and B.4 .

sections.heading: Inertial Confinement Fusion (ICF) laser pulse optimization.
sections.text: In ICF, a precisely shaped laser pulse drives the implosion of a deuterium-tritium fuel capsule to achieve thermonuclear ignition. The design variable x ∈ ℝ 256 x\in\mathbb{R}^{256} is a temporal laser power profile discretized into 256 time steps, and the conditioning signal c c encodes target specifications ( c fix c_{\mathrm{fix}} , 7 dimensions) and 20 performance metrics ( c opt c_{\mathrm{opt}} ) derived from LILAC, the radiation-hydrodynamics simulation code used for inertial-confinement-fusion design studies. At inference, D2C optimizes the 20 performance targets to steer the proposer toward higher-yield pulses. The primary objective is to maximize neutron yield, subject to constraints on pulse energy conservation (the integral of the optimized pulse must match the reference), temporal smoothness (to ensure manufacturability), and spectral fidelity (the frequency content must remain physically plausible). Designs that violate these constraints are operationally unsafe and cannot be fielded on a real facility; the concrete validation criteria are detailed in Appendix C .

sections.heading: Data center workload scheduling.
sections.text: For this task we follow the SustainDC [ 24 ] framework where the goal is to reduce the carbon footprint of large-scale data centers, which requires scheduling computational workloads to exploit temporal variations in grid carbon intensity and cooling efficiency. Here, x ∈ ℝ 144 x\in\mathbb{R}^{144} is a 24-hour workload power profile at 10-minute resolution, and c c encodes environmental state variables ( c fix c_{\mathrm{fix}} , 73 dimensions: ambient temperatures, cooling set-points, IT demand) and energy metrics ( c opt c_{\mathrm{opt}} , 10 dimensions: total power, carbon intensity, etc.). At inference, D2C optimizes the 10 energy metric targets to minimize emissions. The objective is to minimize operational carbon emissions while satisfying a hard workload conservation constraint: the total compute delivered must equal the demand (the integral of the optimized profile must match the reference within a tight tolerance). Additional constraints include inlet temperature safety limits. Final designs are validated against the full SustainDC thermal model (Appendix C ).

sections.heading: 4.2 Design-Bench Benchmarks
sections.text: To position D2C among established MBO methods, we evaluate on four tasks from Design-Bench [ 30 ] : Ant Morphology (continuous, 60-d), D’Kitty Morphology (continuous, 56-d), TF Bind 8 (discrete, 8-d), and TF Bind 10 (discrete, 10-d). These tasks span transcription factor binding (DNA sequence design) and robot morphology optimization, providing a diverse testbed for offline optimization from fixed datasets. The goal in each task is to maximize a black-box oracle score using only the offline dataset.

sections.heading: 4.3 Baselines
sections.text: We compare against 12 baselines, 11 of which are commonly used in offline MBO: Gradient Ascent, COMs [ 31 ] , BDI [ 5 ] , CbAS [ 2 ] , MINs [ 19 ] , REINFORCE [ 34 ] , DDOM [ 18 ] , GTG [ 39 ] , PGS [ 3 ] , GP-qEI [ 28 ] , CMA-ES [ 13 ] , and Brute Force, a diffusion-based approach that replaces gradient-based conditioning optimization with a forward-only sweep over c opt c_{\mathrm{opt}} (Appendix A ). For the real-world tasks, all surrogate-based baselines share the same frozen S ϕ S_{\phi} .

sections.heading: Design-Bench tasks.
sections.text: D2C achieves the best average rank across the four Design-Bench tasks, placing first on TF Bind 8 and TF Bind 10, second on D’Kitty, and third on Ant. We therefore position D2C as robust across standard MBO benchmarks, with the strongest overall performance by average rank. Additional ablations on guidance scale (including its selection without oracle access), optimization steps, learning rate, DDIM steps, optimizable conditioning dimensionality, conditioning versus latent-noise optimization, constraint-satisfying improvement rate, candidate budget, and computational cost are reported in Section D . In particular, with the proposer, surrogate, and evaluation protocol held fixed, optimizing the conditioning outperforms optimizing the latent noise on both real-world tasks (Section D.7 ).

sections.heading: 5 Related Work
sections.text: Offline model-based optimization (MBO) seeks high-scoring designs using only a fixed dataset, with no online evaluations [ 30 ] . Existing approaches include forward methods that optimize a learned surrogate in design space [ 31 , 9 , 36 , 37 , 4 ] , inverse methods that map target scores to designs with increasingly expressive generators [ 2 , 7 , 19 , 16 , 18 ] , and trajectory-based methods that learn to improve from synthetic optimization paths [ 23 , 3 , 39 ] . Forward methods remain limited by surrogate extrapolation, while inverse and trajectory-based methods typically keep the conditioning target fixed at inference time rather than refining it against downstream objectives. Recent diffusion-based optimization methods attempt to integrate optimization feedback into generation, including guided warm-starts with Langevin corrections [ 17 ] , uncertainty-aware conditioning selection [ 35 ] , editing-based optimization against pseudo-targets [ 38 ] , and end-to-end gradient propagation through diffusion samplers in image-generation settings [ 33 , 27 ] . However, these methods either operate outside offline MBO, rely on post-hoc corrections or heuristic target selection, or do not study physics-informed constrained design with a frozen proposer-evaluator architecture. Unlike these methods, D2C targets offline MBO and treats the deterministic reverse diffusion chain as a differentiable map in the conditioning signal itself, optimizing that conditioning directly against surrogate and physics-based penalty losses, with final validity enforced by domain-specific hard constraints.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion and Limitations
sections.text: We introduced Differentiable Diffusion Conditioning (D2C), a framework that turns a pretrained conditional diffusion model into an end-to-end gradient-based optimizer for physical design. By establishing a practical backpropagation path from composite physics-informed objectives, through a frozen surrogate evaluator, back through the deterministic DDIM reverse chain to the conditioning input, D2C enables gradient-based optimization without retraining or fine-tuning the generative model. The composed proposer-evaluator architecture of D2C helps keep generated designs closer to the empirical data distribution induced by the learned prior under appropriately tuned guidance while the surrogate provides directional gradient signals, helping reduce the out-of-distribution exploitation that plagues direct surrogate optimization. Across two real-world scientific tasks and four Design-Bench tasks, D2C delivers the strongest results on the real-world tasks and the best average rank across the benchmark suite.

sections.heading: 6.1 Limitations
sections.text: • Computational cost. D2C requires backpropagation through a T T -step DDIM chain at each optimization iteration, making it roughly 8 8 – 17 × 17\times slower than single-pass methods (Table 16 ). While our ablations show that T T and J J can be reduced with minimal quality loss, the method remains unsuitable for latency-critical applications. • Surrogate dependence. The quality of the gradient signal is bounded by the accuracy of the frozen surrogate S ϕ S_{\phi} . In regimes where the surrogate is poorly calibrated, the optimization may converge to high-scoring surrogate designs that perform poorly on the true objective. Future work could incorporate uncertainty quantification into the surrogate to mitigate this. • Validity-first selection. D2C combines differentiable penalties with a final validity-first selection step. As a result, method quality should be interpreted jointly through both achieved gain and the rate at which valid improving solutions are found. • Domain-specific tuning. While D2C is broadly applicable, the choice of loss terms, constraint definitions, and optimization hyperparameters requires domain expertise and may involve trial-and-error tuning for new applications. Appendix I provides extended practical guidance.

sections.heading: A.1 Computational Resources
sections.text: All experiments were conducted on a node equipped with four NVIDIA H100 GPUs. Training the diffusion proposer and the surrogate evaluator together on a single GPU takes approximately 20 hours per training run. For the optimization time on this same hardware please refer to Subsection D.10 .

sections.heading: A.2 Diffusion Proposer Architecture
sections.text: The proposer G θ G_{\theta} is an MLP-based epsilon-prediction network. Both ICF and DC tasks use the same architecture design; only the input/output dimensionalities and hidden width differ. sections.heading: A.6 Baselines Implementations and Hyperparameters
sections.text: For the Design-Bench tasks, baseline implementations and hyperparameters are sourced from the official design-baselines repository 1 1 1 https://github.com/brandontrabucco/design-baselines , the GTG authors’ implementation 2 2 2 https://github.com/dbsxodud-11/GTG , and the DDOM authors’ implementation 3 3 3 https://github.com/siddarthk97/ddom . All baselines use the hyperparameters from their respective repositories. For the real-world tasks , we implement all baselines that require a surrogate model using the same frozen S ϕ S_{\phi} to ensure a fair comparison. For approaches that require training a neural network or diffusion model for test-time optimization, we use the same hidden dimension as our proposer when applicable. For gradient-based baselines, we perform grid search over learning rates { 5 × 10 − 4 , 1 × 10 − 3 , 5 × 10 − 3 , 1 × 10 − 2 , 5 × 10 − 2 } \{5\times 10^{-4},1\times 10^{-3},5\times 10^{-3},1\times 10^{-2},5\times 10^{-2}\} and select the best-performing value for each method and task. For the evolutionary baseline CMA-ES, we use the cma Python package with default hyperparameters except for population size. For GP-qEI, we use a Gaussian Process surrogate with a Matérn kernel ( ν = 2.5 \nu=2.5 ). For the diffusion-based Brute Force baseline on the real-world tasks, we do not perform a single one-shot DDIM sample. Instead, we reuse the same frozen proposer as D2C but replace gradient-based conditioning updates with an explicit sweep over hand-chosen conditioning directions. On ICF, the baseline linearly increases the yield-related conditioning coordinate and runs one full DDIM rollout at each sweep point, retaining the best candidate that passes the same gain, area, FFT, and correlation checks used for D2C. On DC, it linearly decreases selected energy-metric conditioning coordinates and runs repeated DDIM rollouts for multiple noise seeds at each sweep point, followed by the same workload-conservation and inlet-temperature checks used for D2C. Thus, Brute Force should be interpreted as a forward-only conditioning sweep with many repeated DDIM generations, not as a single batched generation pass. For the surrogate-optimized real-world baselines, we do not optimize the primary objective alone. To reduce the chance that differences in constraint-satisfying improvement rate are an artifact of objective-only optimization, Gradient Ascent, REINFORCE, and CMA-ES are augmented with domain-aligned penalties or projections that mirror the main constraint families used by D2C, although these baselines operate directly in design space or in low-dimensional latent parameterizations rather than through the conditioning optimization of Eq. 13 . On ICF, Gradient Ascent maximizes surrogate-predicted yield while adding similarity and first/second-order smoothness regularization, REINFORCE uses reward terms for yield together with area and spectral penalties, and CMA-ES searches in a PCA-reduced pulse space with an objective that combines surrogate-predicted yield with similarity, area, and squared first-difference penalties, together with a hard projection that prevents pulse area from exceeding the reference; all three are then validated using the same gain, area, FFT, and correlation thresholds as D2C. On DC, Gradient Ascent minimizes surrogate-predicted carbon emissions with area-conservation and similarity penalties, REINFORCE uses carbon-reduction reward together with an area-conservation penalty, and CMA-ES searches in a PCA-reduced profile space with carbon-reduction objective plus area-conservation, similarity, and squared first-difference penalties; all three are then filtered by the same workload-conservation and inlet-temperature constraints used for D2C. Thus, the lower constraint-satisfying improvement rates of these baselines in Table 14 should not be interpreted as evidence that they ignore constraint-aware optimization entirely. For all real-world baselines, hyperparameters were selected on the validation split only, and the test split was used exclusively for final reporting.

sections.heading: B.1 ICF
sections.text: The training dataset comprises ∼ 2,600,000 {\sim}2{,}600{,}000 radiation-hydrodynamics simulations from the LILAC simulation database. Each sample consists of a 256-dimensional laser pulse profile and 27 conditioning dimensions (7 target parameters + 20 LILAC performance variables). The data are split into 80% training, 10% validation, and 10% test ( ∼ 260,000 {\sim}260{,}000 samples each). The validation set was used for hyperparameter tuning; the test set is used exclusively for final evaluation. We randomly sample 2,000 pulses from the test set and use the same 2,000 for all methods. ICF Top selects the 1,000 highest-yield samples from the test set. The surrogate S ϕ S_{\phi} achieves < 1 % <1\% WMAPE on all 20 predicted LILAC variables.

sections.heading: B.1.1 ICF Data Generation
sections.text: The ICF dataset is generated from radiation-hydrodynamics simulations (LILAC code), where each simulation is specified by a target design and a laser pulse shape. LILAC is a prominent one-dimensional Lagrangian hydrodynamics ICF code [ 12 , 32 , 6 , 20 , 10 , 11 ] . The laser pulse shape is prescribed via an internal library that parameterizes it into descriptive features such as inter-pulse time delays between Gaussian-shaped components, maximum power, and total energy. The full input specification thus lives in a 27-dimensional parameter space consisting of target specifications and a parameterized laser-pulse description. Although this 27-D space permits uniform sampling subject to physical constraints (e.g., maximum laser energy, allowable target thicknesses), such sampling does not reflect how experiments or simulations are actually designed. In practice, high-performing implosions occupy only a small region of this high-dimensional space, guided by physics intent rather than being distributed uniformly across the full admissible hypervolume. The region of desirable inputs therefore lies on a lower-dimensional manifold embedded within the 27-D space, a manifold that is not explicitly known or parameterized but emerges from complex physics couplings between target geometry and laser-pulse features. To sample this manifold more effectively, we supplement random draws with perturbations of known high-performing implosion designs. Perturbing their laser-pulse features and target parameters produces a family of nearby points that remain close to the underlying physics manifold while still providing variation in implosion performance. This strategy captures the empirical observation that, for a fixed target specification, laser-pulse shapes close to physics-informed designs typically outperform large random perturbations. The resulting dataset therefore reflects a distribution with multiple high-performance clusters concentrated on an unknown manifold within the 27-D input space, rather than a uniform distribution over the full hypervolume. Note: The fusion dataset and simulation code fall under US export-control regulations. Certain implementation details and the data cannot be publicly released. Interested parties may contact the authors; data may be shared upon reasonable request with parties who have the appropriate permissions and legal authorization to access this class of controlled data.

sections.heading: B.2 ICF Oracle Evaluator
sections.text: At test time, optimized ICF pulse designs are scored by a separate high-accuracy LILAC-validated evaluation surrogate that is distinct from the frozen optimization-time surrogate. This evaluation oracle is trained on the full available ICF dataset and is used only for final offline scoring, not for optimization. It should therefore be interpreted as a best-available simulator proxy trained on all available offline data for final comparison, rather than as a held-out model used within the optimization loop. Because this evaluation oracle is distinct from the frozen optimization-time surrogate, the final reported scores are not obtained by reusing the same model that provides gradients during optimization. The oracle achieves < < 1% weighted mean absolute percentage error (WMAPE) on all 20 LILAC performance variables when compared against LILAC radiation-hydrodynamics simulation outputs. This level of accuracy indicates that the reported yield gains are a close proxy for relative trends predicted by the underlying physics code.

sections.heading: Why not evaluate with LILAC directly?
sections.text: Direct online evaluation with the LILAC simulator is infeasible at the scale required in this study because simulator access requires advanced scheduling, computational allocation, and substantial preparation. We therefore use a separate high-accuracy evaluation surrogate for final offline scoring. This introduces a proxy-evaluation limitation, but the same evaluation oracle is used for D2C and all baselines, making the large-scale comparison internally fair under a common scoring rule. Because the oracle has sub-1% error relative to LILAC simulation outputs, it provides a practical and informative approximation for large-scale comparison. This separation between optimization-time surrogate and evaluation-time oracle does not eliminate proxy-evaluation bias, but it reduces the risk that reported gains are merely artifacts of the optimization surrogate itself. In addition to this large-scale oracle-based evaluation, we performed a separate small-scale LILAC validation on 20 high-yield expert-designed pulses. Here, expert-designed refers to pulses manually designed by ICF experts based on expert knowledge. Using the same D2C conditioning-optimization approach, we observed an average yield gain of 9.8% relative to the original expert pulse baselines. Because this direct-simulator check is small-scale, we treat it as supplementary corroboration rather than the primary quantitative basis for the large-scale comparison.

sections.heading: B.3 DC
sections.text: The training dataset comprises 200,000 200{,}000 data center operating scenarios generated from the SustainDC physics-based thermal and energy simulator [ 24 ] . The simulator computes rack-level IT power, HVAC power, cooling tower fan power, compressor load, and thermal state from workload profiles and carbon footprints. We seed the generation with real workload traces from the Alibaba cluster dataset [ 1 ] and region-specific carbon intensity and weather profiles for Arizona (AZ), California (CA), and New York (NY), both provided within the SustainDC framework. We augment with synthetic variations of workload patterns, carbon footprint schedules, and CRAC set-point profiles to ensure broad distributional coverage. The three geographic regions provide diverse grid carbon intensities and climate conditions, enabling the model to generalize across different operational regimes. Each sample consists of a 144-dimensional workload power profile (24h at 10-min resolution) and 83 conditioning dimensions (73 environment state variables + 10 energy metrics). The data are split into 80% training, 10% validation, and 10% test ( ∼ 20,000 {\sim}20{,}000 samples each). Following the same protocol as ICF, all hyperparameter selection is performed on the validation set; the test set is reserved for final reporting. We randomly sample 2,000 scenarios from the test set and use the same 2,000 for all methods. Final designs are validated against the full physics-based model (not the surrogate). We use the public SustainDC codebase, whose repository documentation states that the project is primarily released under the MIT License, with some derived portions attributed to CarbonExplorer under CC BY-NC 4.0; we use and cite that code under the stated repository terms. 4 4 4 https://github.com/HewlettPackard/dc-rl

sections.heading: B.4 Design-Bench
sections.text: We use the standard offline-subset protocol of Design-Bench [ 30 ] : each method trains on the bottom p p -th percentile of the full dataset by y y -value (50% for TF Bind 8/10, 40% for Ant/D’Kitty Morphology), and y y -normalization uses full-dataset bounds so that the best offline design scores below 1. The public Design-Bench codebase used for these tasks is released under the MIT License, and we use and cite the benchmark under that license. 5 5 5 https://github.com/brandontrabucco/design-bench For Design-Bench, D2C uses a task-specific variant of the inference-time optimization procedure because the conditional input is only a single scalar target score. In this setting, directly optimizing the conditioning provides only limited control. We therefore fix the conditioning to a high normalized target score ( c = 1.0 c{=}1.0 ) and instead optimize the initial latent/noise vector through the deterministic DDIM chain using gradients from the frozen surrogate. Empirically, this latent-optimization variant performed better on Design-Bench than direct optimization of the one-dimensional conditioning input. In contrast, for ICF and DC we retain direct conditioning optimization because those domains expose multiple optimizable conditioning coordinates; on those tasks, conditioning optimization outperforms latent-noise optimization (Section D.7 ). sections.heading: Appendix C Domain-Specific Constraints
sections.text: After conditioning optimization (Section 3.6 ), each candidate design is validated against a set of domain-specific hard physical constraints before selection. These constraints are not a property of the D2C framework itself but reflect the safety-critical requirements of each application domain. Only candidates that pass all constraints are eligible for selection by primary objective; this ensures that reported improvements correspond to physically realizable and operationally safe designs.

sections.heading: ICF laser pulse constraints.
sections.text: A candidate pulse x ^ 0 \hat{x}_{0} is deemed valid if it satisfies all four of the following conditions simultaneously: 1. Yield gain. The surrogate-predicted neutron yield must exceed the baseline yield by at least a minimum threshold: ( Y ^ − Y ref ) / Y ref ≥ δ gain (\hat{Y}-Y_{\mathrm{ref}})/Y_{\mathrm{ref}}\geq\delta_{\mathrm{gain}} , with δ gain = 0.1 % \delta_{\mathrm{gain}}=0.1\% . 2. Energy conservation. The integral of the generated pulse must not exceed that of the reference pulse (with a small tolerance ϵ = 0.01 \epsilon=0.01 ): ∫ x ^ 0 ​ ( t ) ​ 𝑑 t ≤ ∫ x ref ​ ( t ) ​ 𝑑 t + ϵ \int\hat{x}_{0}(t)\,dt\leq\int x_{\mathrm{ref}}(t)\,dt+\epsilon . sections.heading: Appendix E Domain-Specific Training Losses
sections.text: We instantiate the general training objective (Eq. 8 ) for each application domain. In both cases the total loss follows the same four-term structure: denoising, reconstruction, physics-based fidelity, and surrogate consistency. The differences lie in the specific fidelity constraints and surrogate architecture.

sections.heading: E.1 ICF Laser Pulse Optimization
sections.text: The design x ∈ ℝ 256 x\in\mathbb{R}^{256} is a laser power pulse profile, conditioned on c = ( T 0 , … , T 6 , L 1 , … , L 20 ) ∈ ℝ 27 c=(T_{0},\ldots,T_{6},L_{1},\ldots,L_{20})\in\mathbb{R}^{27} , where T i T_{i} are target parameters and L j L_{j} are the 20 LILAC-simulated performance variables included in the conditioning vector.

sections.heading: Surrogate consistency (LILAC).
sections.text: The frozen LILAC surrogate S ϕ ICF S_{\phi}^{\mathrm{ICF}} takes as input the concatenation [ x ^ 0 , c fix ] ∈ ℝ 256 + 7 [\hat{x}_{0},\,c_{\mathrm{fix}}]\in\mathbb{R}^{256+7} (predicted pulse and the 7 target parameters) and predicts 20 LILAC performance variables L ^ ∈ ℝ 20 \hat{L}\in\mathbb{R}^{20} . The loss is: ℒ surr ICF = ‖ L ^ − L ‖ 2 , L ^ = S ϕ ICF ​ ( x ^ 0 , c fix ) , \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{surr}}^{\mathrm{ICF}}=\|\hat{L}-L\|^{2},\qquad\hat{L}=S_{\phi}^{\mathrm{ICF}}(\hat{x}_{0},\,c_{\mathrm{fix}}), (16) where L = ( c 8 , … , c 27 ) ∈ ℝ 20 L=(c_{8},\ldots,c_{27})\in\mathbb{R}^{20} are the ground-truth LILAC variables from the conditioning vector. This loss is applied with weight α s = 1.0 \alpha_{s}=1.0 .

sections.heading: Physics-based fidelity.
sections.text: Two one-sided penalties encourage physical realizability of the generated pulse: ℒ fid ICF = [ ∫ x ^ 0 ​ ( t ) ⋅ s y ​ 𝑑 t − ∫ x ⁡ ( t ) ⋅ s y ​ 𝑑 t ] + + [ max ⁡ ( x ^ 0 ⋅ s y ) − V max ] + , \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{fid}}^{\mathrm{ICF}}=\Bigl[\int\hat{x}_{0}(t)\cdot s_{y}\,dt-\int x(t)\cdot s_{y}\,dt\Bigr]_{+}+\bigl[\max(\hat{x}_{0}\cdot s_{y})-V_{\max}\bigr]_{+}, (17) where s y s_{y} is the data scaler that maps normalized values back to physical units, V max V_{\max} is the maximum observed pulse amplitude, and [ ⋅ ] + = max ⁡ ( ⋅ , 0 ) [\cdot]_{+}=\max(\cdot,0) . The first term prevents the generated pulse from delivering more energy than the reference; the second prevents physically impossible peak powers.

sections.heading: Total ICF training loss.
sections.text: ℒ train ICF = ‖ ϵ − ϵ θ ‖ 2 + α r ​ ‖ x ^ 0 − x ‖ 2 + ℒ surr ICF + α a ​ ℒ fid ICF + α sm ​ ℒ smooth , \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{train}}^{\mathrm{ICF}}=\|\epsilon-\epsilon_{\theta}\|^{2}+\alpha_{r}\,\|\hat{x}_{0}-x\|^{2}+\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{surr}}^{\mathrm{ICF}}+\alpha_{a}\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{fid}}^{\mathrm{ICF}}+\alpha_{\mathrm{sm}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{smooth}}, (18) with weights α r = 0.5 \alpha_{r}=0.5 , α a = 0.001 \alpha_{a}=0.001 , α sm = 0.0001 \alpha_{\mathrm{sm}}=0.0001 .

sections.heading: E.2 Data Center Workload Scheduling
sections.text: The design x ∈ ℝ 144 x\in\mathbb{R}^{144} is a 24-hour workload power profile at 10-minute resolution, conditioned on c ∈ ℝ 83 c\in\mathbb{R}^{83} comprising 73 environment state dimensions ( C 0 , C 1 , C 3 ∈ ℝ 24 C_{0},C_{1},C_{3}\in\mathbb{R}^{24} hourly profiles and C 2 C_{2} scalar IT demand) and 10 energy performance metrics ( E 0 , … , E 9 E_{0},\ldots,E_{9} ).

sections.heading: Surrogate consistency.
sections.text: The frozen DC surrogate S ϕ DC S_{\phi}^{\mathrm{DC}} takes the concatenation [ x ^ 0 , c fix ] ∈ ℝ 144 + 73 [\hat{x}_{0},\,c_{\mathrm{fix}}]\in\mathbb{R}^{144+73} (predicted profile and the 73 environment conditioning dimensions) and predicts 10 energy metrics E ^ ∈ ℝ 10 \hat{E}\in\mathbb{R}^{10} : ℒ surr DC = ‖ E ^ − E ‖ 2 , E ^ = S ϕ DC ​ ( x ^ 0 , c fix ) , \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{surr}}^{\mathrm{DC}}=\|\hat{E}-E\|^{2},\qquad\hat{E}=S_{\phi}^{\mathrm{DC}}(\hat{x}_{0},\,c_{\mathrm{fix}}), (19) where E = ( c 74 , … , c 83 ) ∈ ℝ 10 E=(c_{74},\ldots,c_{83})\in\mathbb{R}^{10} are the ground-truth metrics from the conditioning.

sections.heading: Physics-based fidelity.
sections.text: The fidelity term enforces workload integral conservation and amplitude bounds: ℒ fid DC = [ ∫ x ^ 0 ​ ( t ) ⋅ M ​ 𝑑 t − ∫ x ⁡ ( t ) ⋅ M ​ 𝑑 t ] + + [ max ⁡ ( x ^ 0 ) − 1 ] + + [ − min ⁡ ( x ^ 0 ) ] + , \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{fid}}^{\mathrm{DC}}=\Bigl[\int\hat{x}_{0}(t)\cdot M\,dt-\int x(t)\cdot M\,dt\Bigr]_{+}+\bigl[\max(\hat{x}_{0})-1\bigr]_{+}+\bigl[-\min(\hat{x}_{0})\bigr]_{+}, (20) where M M is the data-range scaling factor. The first term prevents the scheduled workload from exceeding the reference demand; the second and third keep the normalized profile within [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] . This training-stage relaxation is intentionally one-sided: the reconstruction term already anchors samples near observed workloads, so the fidelity term mainly suppresses unrealistic demand inflation while preserving coverage of the empirical profile manifold.

sections.heading: Total DC training loss.

sections.text: We instantiate the general inference-time loss (Eq. 13 ) for each application domain. sections.text: In our framework, each of the N λ N_{\lambda} weight vectors 𝝀 ( m ) ∼ Dir ⁡ ( 𝟏 K ) \boldsymbol{\lambda}^{(m)}\sim\mathrm{Dir}(\mathbf{1}_{K}) defines a different scalarization of the multi-objective loss (Eq. 13 ). Some draws will heavily weight the surrogate yield objective (exploring aggressive performance gains); others will emphasize constraint penalties (producing conservative but highly feasible designs); yet others will balance smoothness against performance. By optimizing N λ N_{\lambda} trajectories in parallel with different weight vectors, the candidate pool explores diverse scalarized trade-offs without requiring manual tuning of fixed weights. This uniformity is with respect to the weight simplex over these task-specific scalarizations; it is not a claim that Dirichlet weighting alone removes arbitrary objective-scale mismatches without the loss design described above. The validity-first selection (Stage 3 of Algorithm 1 ) then picks the best feasible candidate from this diverse pool, combining broad exploration with strict constraint satisfaction.

sections.heading: Appendix I Practical Guidance for Design Optimization with D2C
sections.text: D2C is designed for settings where (i) evaluations of the true objective are expensive (physical simulations, wet-lab experiments, or large-scale facility tests), (ii) hard physical constraints must be satisfied for safety or feasibility, and (iii) offline datasets of moderate size are available. Below we summarize the settings where the method is most compelling, together with regimes where simpler alternatives may sometimes be sufficient.

sections.heading: Settings Well Suited to D2C.
sections.text: • High-cost physical systems with expensive evaluations. D2C is most valuable when each ground-truth evaluation costs hours of compute (e.g., radiation-hydrodynamics simulations) or involves irreversible physical consequences (e.g., laser shots on a fusion facility, equipment management in data centers). The offline training investment is amortized over many test-time optimizations. • Multi-objective problems with hard constraints. The framework naturally accommodates competing objectives and strict feasibility requirements through the composite loss and validity-first selection. If your application has safety-critical constraints that cannot be violated, D2C provides explicit mechanisms to enforce them. • High-dimensional or strongly structured designs. The diffusion proposer excels at generating designs with complex internal structure (temporal profiles, spatial fields) that naive gradient ascent in design space often cannot capture robustly. If the design space has strong correlations or manifold structure, the learned prior is especially beneficial. • Settings where a reliable surrogate exists. The method requires a differentiable surrogate S ϕ S_{\phi} that is accurate in the region of interest. If surrogate error is low ( < 5 % <5\% relative error), the gradient signal is informative.

sections.heading: Settings Where Simpler Alternatives May Suffice.
sections.text: • Low-dimensional problems with weak structure or cheap evaluation. If the design space is very small, the constraints are mild, and evaluations are cheap enough to support direct search or standard Bayesian optimization, then methods such as GP-qEI, CMA-ES, or even brute-force search may be simpler to deploy and sufficiently effective. This is not a blanket limitation of D2C: even in lower-dimensional settings, the method can still be worthwhile when evaluations are expensive, feasibility is safety-critical, or data-distribution-aware generation and validity-first selection materially improve robustness. • Cheap online evaluations available. If the true objective can be queried cheaply and repeatedly, online methods (reinforcement learning, active learning) are often preferable because they can adapt directly to fresh evaluations. D2C is designed for settings with no online evaluation access at test time. • Severely miscalibrated surrogates. If the surrogate is unreliable in the optimization region, gradient-based methods can exploit those inaccuracies. The diffusion prior and validity checks mitigate this to some extent by constraining designs toward the empirical data distribution, but a fundamentally miscalibrated surrogate can still misdirect optimization. • Latency-critical applications. D2C requires backpropagation through a T T -step DDIM chain at each of J J optimization iterations. On current hardware, this takes 30–60 seconds per test sample. If sub-second inference is required, single-pass methods (MINs, DDOM) may be a better fit despite their weaker optimization and constraint-handling performance.

sections.heading: Practical considerations.
sections.text: • Surrogate investment. We recommend training the surrogate to convergence with proper validation, achieving < 2 % <2\% error before proceeding to diffusion model training. • Guidance scale sensitivity. The guidance scale w w is domain-dependent and must be tuned. Domains with tight physical constraints (e.g., ICF) are highly sensitive to w > 2 w>2 ; smoother landscapes (e.g., DC) are more tolerant. Start with w = 2 w=2 and sweep { 1 , 2 , 3 , 5 } \{1,2,3,5\} . The sweep does not require oracle access: ranking w w by the surrogate-predicted gain of candidates that pass the geometric validity checks recovers the oracle-selected value (Section D.2 ). • Noise trials vs. optimization steps. When compute budget is fixed, we find it more effective to increase noise trials N z N_{z} (broader coverage) than optimization steps J J (deeper optimization per trial). Diminishing returns on J J set in after 50–100 steps for most problems. • Constraint design. Hard constraints should be expressed as differentiable penalty terms in the loss wherever possible. Non-differentiable constraints (e.g., discrete feasibility checks) should be handled via the post-hoc validity filter rather than incorporated into the gradient-based loop.

sections.heading: Appendix J Broader Impact
sections.text: As a general offline design-optimization method, D2C could have positive impact in domains where evaluations are expensive and constrained operation matters, such as reducing carbon-footprint in data centers or accelerating scientific design loops while lowering simulation cost. More broadly, methods that keep optimization closer to the empirical data distribution captured by a learned prior while exposing explicit validity checks help reduce unrealistic proposals relative to unconstrained surrogate optimization. Potential negative impacts are also application-specific. The same optimization machinery could be used in domains where accelerating design search is undesirable or access should be restricted.

sections.heading: NeurIPS Paper Checklist
sections.text: 1. Claims Question: Do the main claims made in the abstract and introduction accurately reflect the paper’s contributions and scope? Answer: [Yes] Justification: See the abstract, Section 1, and Sections 4–5; the claims are scoped to offline physics-informed optimization and the reported experiments. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the abstract and introduction do not include the claims made in the paper. • The abstract and/or introduction should clearly state the claims made, including the contributions made in the paper and important assumptions and limitations. A [No] or [N/A] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers. • The claims made should match theoretical and experimental results, and reflect how much the results can be expected to generalize to other settings. • It is fine to include aspirational goals as motivation as long as it is clear that these goals are not attained by the paper. 2. Limitations Question: Does the paper discuss the limitations of the work performed by the authors? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Section 5 discusses computational cost, surrogate dependence, validity-first selection, and domain-specific tuning. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper has no limitation while the answer [No] means that the paper has limitations, but those are not discussed in the paper. • The authors are encouraged to create a separate “Limitations” section in their paper. • The paper should point out any strong assumptions and how robust the results are to violations of these assumptions (e.g., independence assumptions, noiseless settings, model well-specification, asymptotic approximations only holding locally). The authors should reflect on how these assumptions might be violated in practice and what the implications would be. • The authors should reflect on the scope of the claims made, e.g., if the approach was only tested on a few datasets or with a few runs. In general, empirical results often depend on implicit assumptions, which should be articulated. • The authors should reflect on the factors that influence the performance of the approach. For example, a facial recognition algorithm may perform poorly when image resolution is low or images are taken in low lighting. Or a speech-to-text system might not be used reliably to provide closed captions for online lectures because it fails to handle technical jargon. • The authors should discuss the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithms and how they scale with dataset size. • If applicable, the authors should discuss possible limitations of their approach to address problems of privacy and fairness. • While the authors might fear that complete honesty about limitations might be used by reviewers as grounds for rejection, a worse outcome might be that reviewers discover limitations that aren’t acknowledged in the paper. The authors should use their best judgment and recognize that individual actions in favor of transparency play an important role in developing norms that preserve the integrity of the community. Reviewers will be specifically instructed to not penalize honesty concerning limitations. 3. Theory assumptions and proofs Question: For each theoretical result, does the paper provide the full set of assumptions and a complete (and correct) proof? Answer: [N/A] Justification: The paper does not include theoretical results. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include theoretical results. • All the theorems, formulas, and proofs in the paper should be numbered and cross-referenced. • All assumptions should be clearly stated or referenced in the statement of any theorems. • The proofs can either appear in the main paper or the supplemental material, but if they appear in the supplemental material, the authors are encouraged to provide a short proof sketch to provide intuition. • Inversely, any informal proof provided in the core of the paper should be complemented by formal proofs provided in appendix or supplemental material. • Theorems and Lemmas that the proof relies upon should be properly referenced. 4. Experimental result reproducibility Question: Does the paper fully disclose all the information needed to reproduce the main experimental results of the paper to the extent that it affects the main claims and/or conclusions of the paper (regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not)? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Sections 4–6 and the appendix specify datasets, splits, losses, hyperparameters, baselines, evaluation, and ablation settings. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. • If the paper includes experiments, a [No] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers: Making the paper reproducible is important, regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not. • If the contribution is a dataset and/or model, the authors should describe the steps taken to make their results reproducible or verifiable. • Depending on the contribution, reproducibility can be accomplished in various ways. For example, if the contribution is a novel architecture, describing the architecture fully might suffice, or if the contribution is a specific model and empirical evaluation, it may be necessary to either make it possible for others to replicate the model with the same dataset, or provide access to the model. In general. releasing code and data is often one good way to accomplish this, but reproducibility can also be provided via detailed instructions for how to replicate the results, access to a hosted model (e.g., in the case of a large language model), releasing of a model checkpoint, or other means that are appropriate to the research performed. • While NeurIPS does not require releasing code, the conference does require all submissions to provide some reasonable avenue for reproducibility, which may depend on the nature of the contribution. For example (a) If the contribution is primarily a new algorithm, the paper should make it clear how to reproduce that algorithm. (b) If the contribution is primarily a new model architecture, the paper should describe the architecture clearly and fully. (c) If the contribution is a new model (e.g., a large language model), then there should either be a way to access this model for reproducing the results or a way to reproduce the model (e.g., with an open-source dataset or instructions for how to construct the dataset). (d) We recognize that reproducibility may be tricky in some cases, in which case authors are welcome to describe the particular way they provide for reproducibility. In the case of closed-source models, it may be that access to the model is limited in some way (e.g., to registered users), but it should be possible for other researchers to have some path to reproducing or verifying the results. 5. Open access to data and code Question: Does the paper provide open access to the data and code, with sufficient instructions to faithfully reproduce the main experimental results, as described in supplemental material? Answer: [Yes] Justification: We provide the code used for DC and design-bench attached in the supplementary material. The ICF data and its artifacts are export controlled and cannot be publicly shared (Appendix, ICF data generation). Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that paper does not include experiments requiring code. • Please see the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines ( https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy ) for more details. • While we encourage the release of code and data, we understand that this might not be possible, so [No] is an acceptable answer. Papers cannot be rejected simply for not including code, unless this is central to the contribution (e.g., for a new open-source benchmark). • The instructions should contain the exact command and environment needed to run to reproduce the results. See the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines ( https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy ) for more details. • The authors should provide instructions on data access and preparation, including how to access the raw data, preprocessed data, intermediate data, and generated data, etc. • The authors should provide scripts to reproduce all experimental results for the new proposed method and baselines. If only a subset of experiments are reproducible, they should state which ones are omitted from the script and why. • At submission time, to preserve anonymity, the authors should release anonymized versions (if applicable). • Providing as much information as possible in supplemental material (appended to the paper) is recommended, but including URLs to data and code is permitted. 6. Experimental setting/details Question: Does the paper specify all the training and test details (e.g., data splits, hyperparameters, how they were chosen, type of optimizer) necessary to understand the results? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Section 4 and Appendix A report the splits, architectures, optimizers, hyperparameters, and model-selection procedures. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. • The experimental setting should be presented in the core of the paper to a level of detail that is necessary to appreciate the results and make sense of them. • The full details can be provided either with the code, in appendix, or as supplemental material. 7. Experiment statistical significance Question: Does the paper report error bars suitably and correctly defined or other appropriate information about the statistical significance of the experiments? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The main results and ablations report mean ± \pm standard deviation over 5 runs; see Section 4.3 and the table captions. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. • The authors should answer [Yes] if the results are accompanied by error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests, at least for the experiments that support the main claims of the paper. • The factors of variability that the error bars are capturing should be clearly stated (for example, train/test split, initialization, random drawing of some parameter, or overall run with given experimental conditions). • The method for calculating the error bars should be explained (closed form formula, call to a library function, bootstrap, etc.) • The assumptions made should be given (e.g., Normally distributed errors). • It should be clear whether the error bar is the standard deviation or the standard error of the mean. • It is OK to report 1-sigma error bars, but one should state it. The authors should preferably report a 2-sigma error bar than state that they have a 96% CI, if the hypothesis of Normality of errors is not verified. • For asymmetric distributions, the authors should be careful not to show in tables or figures symmetric error bars that would yield results that are out of range (e.g., negative error rates). • If error bars are reported in tables or plots, the authors should explain in the text how they were calculated and reference the corresponding figures or tables in the text. 8. Experiments compute resources Question: For each experiment, does the paper provide sufficient information on the computer resources (type of compute workers, memory, time of execution) needed to reproduce the experiments? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Appendix A reports the hardware (four NVIDIA H100 GPUs) and approximate training/optimization costs. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. • The paper should indicate the type of compute workers CPU or GPU, internal cluster, or cloud provider, including relevant memory and storage. • The paper should provide the amount of compute required for each of the individual experimental runs as well as estimate the total compute. • The paper should disclose whether the full research project required more compute than the experiments reported in the paper (e.g., preliminary or failed experiments that didn’t make it into the paper). 9. Code of ethics Question: Does the research conducted in the paper conform, in every respect, with the NeurIPS Code of Ethics https://neurips.cc/public/EthicsGuidelines ? Answer: [Yes] Justification: To the best of our knowledge, yes; the work uses offline data/simulations, involves no human subjects, and discloses relevant release limitations. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the authors have not reviewed the NeurIPS Code of Ethics. • If the authors answer [No] , they should explain the special circumstances that require a deviation from the Code of Ethics. • The authors should make sure to preserve anonymity (e.g., if there is a special consideration due to laws or regulations in their jurisdiction). 10. Broader impacts Question: Does the paper discuss both potential positive societal impacts and negative societal impacts of the work performed? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The appendix now includes a short broader-impact discussion covering potential benefits, misuse risks, and deployment risks of the method. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that there is no societal impact of the work performed. • If the authors answer [N/A] or [No] , they should explain why their work has no societal impact or why the paper does not address societal impact. • Examples of negative societal impacts include potential malicious or unintended uses (e.g., disinformation, generating fake profiles, surveillance), fairness considerations (e.g., deployment of technologies that could make decisions that unfairly impact specific groups), privacy considerations, and security considerations. • The conference expects that many papers will be foundational research and not tied to particular applications, let alone deployments. However, if there is a direct path to any negative applications, the authors should point it out. For example, it is legitimate to point out that an improvement in the quality of generative models could be used to generate Deepfakes for disinformation. On the other hand, it is not needed to point out that a generic algorithm for optimizing neural networks could enable people to train models that generate Deepfakes faster. • The authors should consider possible harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended and functioning correctly, harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended but gives incorrect results, and harms following from (intentional or unintentional) misuse of the technology. • If there are negative societal impacts, the authors could also discuss possible mitigation strategies (e.g., gated release of models, providing defenses in addition to attacks, mechanisms for monitoring misuse, mechanisms to monitor how a system learns from feedback over time, improving the efficiency and accessibility of ML). 11. Safeguards Question: Does the paper describe safeguards that have been put in place for responsible release of data or models that have a high risk for misuse (e.g., pre-trained language models, image generators, or scraped datasets)? Answer: [N/A] Justification: The submission does not release a high-risk model or scraped dataset. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper poses no such risks. • Released models that have a high risk for misuse or dual-use should be released with necessary safeguards to allow for controlled use of the model, for example by requiring that users adhere to usage guidelines or restrictions to access the model or implementing safety filters. • Datasets that have been scraped from the Internet could pose safety risks. The authors should describe how they avoided releasing unsafe images. • We recognize that providing effective safeguards is challenging, and many papers do not require this, but we encourage authors to take this into account and make a best faith effort. 12. Licenses for existing assets Question: Are the creators or original owners of assets (e.g., code, data, models), used in the paper, properly credited and are the license and terms of use explicitly mentioned and properly respected? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The paper credits the public code assets used and explicitly states the Design-Bench and SustainDC repository licenses in the appendix data section. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not use existing assets. • The authors should cite the original paper that produced the code package or dataset. • The authors should state which version of the asset is used and, if possible, include a URL. • The name of the license (e.g., CC-BY 4.0) should be included for each asset. • For scraped data from a particular source (e.g., website), the copyright and terms of service of that source should be provided. • If assets are released, the license, copyright information, and terms of use in the package should be provided. For popular datasets, paperswithcode.com/datasets has curated licenses for some datasets. Their licensing guide can help determine the license of a dataset. • For existing datasets that are re-packaged, both the original license and the license of the derived asset (if it has changed) should be provided. • If this information is not available online, the authors are encouraged to reach out to the asset’s creators. 13. New assets Question: Are new assets introduced in the paper well documented and is the documentation provided alongside the assets? Answer: [N/A] Justification: The paper does not introduce a new publicly released dataset, model, or code asset. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not release new assets. • Researchers should communicate the details of the dataset/code/model as part of their submissions via structured templates. This includes details about training, license, limitations, etc. • The paper should discuss whether and how consent was obtained from people whose asset is used. • At submission time, remember to anonymize your assets (if applicable). You can either create an anonymized URL or include an anonymized zip file. 14. Crowdsourcing and research with human subjects Question: For crowdsourcing experiments and research with human subjects, does the paper include the full text of instructions given to participants and screenshots, if applicable, as well as details about compensation (if any)? Answer: [N/A] Justification: The paper does not involve crowdsourcing or research with human subjects. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not involve crowdsourcing nor research with human subjects. • Including this information in the supplemental material is fine, but if the main contribution of the paper involves human subjects, then as much detail as possible should be included in the main paper. • According to the NeurIPS Code of Ethics, workers involved in data collection, curation, or other labor should be paid at least the minimum wage in the country of the data collector. 15. Institutional review board (IRB) approvals or equivalent for research with human subjects Question: Does the paper describe potential risks incurred by study participants, whether such risks were disclosed to the subjects, and whether Institutional Review Board (IRB) approvals (or an equivalent approval/review based on the requirements of your country or institution) were obtained? Answer: [N/A] Justification: The paper does not involve crowdsourcing or research with human subjects. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not involve crowdsourcing nor research with human subjects. • Depending on the country in which research is conducted, IRB approval (or equivalent) may be required for any human subjects research. If you obtained IRB approval, you should clearly state this in the paper. • We recognize that the procedures for this may vary significantly between institutions and locations, and we expect authors to adhere to the NeurIPS Code of Ethics and the guidelines for their institution. • For initial submissions, do not include any information that would break anonymity (if applicable), such as the institution conducting the review. 16. Declaration of LLM usage Question: Does the paper describe the usage of LLMs if it is an important, original, or non-standard component of the core methods in this research? Note that if the LLM is used only for writing, editing, or formatting purposes and does not impact the core methodology, scientific rigor, or originality of the research, declaration is not required. Answer: [N/A] Justification: The paper does not involve the use of LLMs as an important, original, or non-standard component of the core methods in this research. Affiliation: Hewlett Packard Enterprise Email: alees@lle.rochester.edu Abstract Optimizing high-dimensional physical systems under expensive evaluations and complex constraints is a central challenge in science and engineering. In offline model-based optimization (MBO), methods must improve designs using only a fixed dataset and no test-time access to the true objective. However, existing methods typically suffer from conservatism, unconstrained surrogate exploitation, or function as static inference-time samplers that cannot refine candidates against precise physical objectives. In this paper, we propose Differentiable Diffusion Conditioning (D2C) for offline MBO, which leverages the fact that deterministic sampling makes the reverse denoising chain differentiable with respect to the conditioning signal. D2C turns a frozen conditional diffusion model into an end-to-end gradient-based optimizer by directly optimizing conditioning variables at test time via gradients from frozen surrogate objectives and physics-informed penalties backpropagated through the reverse chain. We implement this idea in a composed proposer-evaluator framework and evaluate it on laser pulse optimization for inertial confinement fusion, sustainable data-center workload scheduling, and four Design-Bench tasks. Our method achieves the strongest results on the two real-world tasks and the best average rank across four Design-Bench tasks. 1 Introduction The optimization of complex physical systems remains one of the most consequential challenges in science and engineering. Problems such as laser pulse shaping for inertial confinement fusion (ICF) and workload scheduling in large-scale data centers share a common structure: objective functions are computationally expensive to evaluate, the design space is high-dimensional with non-linear correlations, and candidate solutions must satisfy strict physical constraints where any violation carries safety-critical consequences. The offline model-based optimization (MBO) paradigm addresses the evaluation-cost bottleneck by learning entirely from a fixed dataset of previously evaluated designs, with no access to the true objective at test time. Within this paradigm, existing approaches fall into three broad families. Forward (surrogate-based) methods train a neural network to approximate the objective and perform gradient ascent in design space [ 31 , 9 ] ; while effective, optimizing directly in unconstrained design space can move into regions poorly supported by the offline data, where the surrogate is unreliable. Inverse methods learn a conditional mapping from target performance labels to designs [ 2 , 19 , 18 , 22 ] ; these tend to stay closer to the empirical data distribution but are limited by the performance ceiling of the training labels and struggle to extrapolate beyond observed optima. Trajectory-based methods construct synthetic improvement paths and train generative models to imitate optimization dynamics [ 3 , 39 ] ; while powerful, they remain inference-time samplers whose conditioning targets are fixed prior to generation, with no mechanism to refine designs against downstream objectives. A common limitation across these families is the lack of a direct, differentiable path from a physics-informed objective back to the generative process. The conditioning signal that steers generation is treated as a static input rather than an optimizable variable. This decoupling is especially limiting in safety-critical physical domains where the objective is not a single scalar score but a composite of performance metrics, conservation laws, and hard feasibility constraints that must be jointly satisfied. We address these limitations by proposing Differentiable Diffusion Conditioning (D2C) for Physics-Informed Optimization, a novel approach that converts a conditional diffusion model into an end-to-end gradient-based optimizer for constrained physical design. Our key insight for offline MBO is that deterministic diffusion sampling renders the reverse chain differentiable with respect to the conditioning input, enabling end-to-end backpropagation from downstream physics-informed objectives, through a frozen surrogate evaluator and physics-informed penalty terms, back to the conditioning variables. D2C therefore optimizes conditioning directly at test time while keeping both the diffusion proposer and surrogate evaluator fixed, yielding a practical end-to-end gradient path from the downstream objective to the conditioning variables. The diffusion model tends to keep candidates closer to the data distribution, while surrogate and physics-informed losses steer them toward feasible, high-performing designs. We embed this mechanism within a composed proposer-evaluator architecture: the diffusion model G θ G_{\theta} (proposer) generates candidates, and a surrogate S ϕ S_{\phi} (evaluator) scores them, with both remaining fixed during test-time optimization. Only the conditioning input is updated, which helps keep optimization closer to the proposer’s learned data distribution while limiting direct surrogate exploitation. A stochastic multi-objective weighting scheme and validity-first selection further encourage broad exploration of competing objective trade-offs while enforcing strict constraint satisfaction. Figure 1 provides an overview of the full D2C pipeline. Our main contributions are: • End-to-End Conditioning Optimization Through Diffusion. We use the deterministic reverse diffusion chain to backpropagate end-to-end from composite physics objectives to the conditioning inputs, making the conditioning signal itself the optimization variable within the generative process; optimizing it outperforms optimizing the latent noise (Appendix D.7 ). • Frozen Proposer-Evaluator Architecture. We introduce a composed proposer-evaluator architecture in which a frozen diffusion proposer helps keep candidates closer to the empirical data distribution, while a frozen surrogate evaluator provides optimization gradients, reducing out-of-distribution exploitation. • Physics-Informed Multi-Objective Optimization. We integrate heterogeneous objectives directly into the differentiable sampling chain via a stochastic Dirichlet-weighted loss, enabling principled multi-objective optimization under domain-specific constraints. • Strong Empirical Performance. D2C achieves the best results on the two real-world physical design tasks and the best average rank across four Design-Bench tasks. Figure 1: Overview of D2C. A frozen conditional diffusion proposer generates designs from conditioning inputs, a frozen surrogate evaluator and physics-informed penalties define a differentiable test-time objective, and gradients are backpropagated through the deterministic DDIM chain to optimize the conditioning signal. Multiple noise trials and loss-weight samples produce a candidate pool, from which the best valid design is selected after domain-specific constraint checks. 2 Preliminaries 2.1 Conditional Denoising Diffusion Models Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPMs) [ 14 ] learn a generative model of a data distribution p ⁡ ( x ) p(x) by reversing a forward noise process. Additional implementation, hyperparameter, and evaluation details are provided in Appendices A and B.4 . 4.1 Real-World Physical Design Tasks Inertial Confinement Fusion (ICF) laser pulse optimization. In ICF, a precisely shaped laser pulse drives the implosion of a deuterium-tritium fuel capsule to achieve thermonuclear ignition. The design variable x ∈ ℝ 256 x\in\mathbb{R}^{256} is a temporal laser power profile discretized into 256 time steps, and the conditioning signal c c encodes target specifications ( c fix c_{\mathrm{fix}} , 7 dimensions) and 20 performance metrics ( c opt c_{\mathrm{opt}} ) derived from LILAC, the radiation-hydrodynamics simulation code used for inertial-confinement-fusion design studies. At inference, D2C optimizes the 20 performance targets to steer the proposer toward higher-yield pulses. The primary objective is to maximize neutron yield, subject to constraints on pulse energy conservation (the integral of the optimized pulse must match the reference), temporal smoothness (to ensure manufacturability), and spectral fidelity (the frequency content must remain physically plausible). Designs that violate these constraints are operationally unsafe and cannot be fielded on a real facility; the concrete validation criteria are detailed in Appendix C . Data center workload scheduling. For this task we follow the SustainDC [ 24 ] framework where the goal is to reduce the carbon footprint of large-scale data centers, which requires scheduling computational workloads to exploit temporal variations in grid carbon intensity and cooling efficiency. Here, x ∈ ℝ 144 x\in\mathbb{R}^{144} is a 24-hour workload power profile at 10-minute resolution, and c c encodes environmental state variables ( c fix c_{\mathrm{fix}} , 73 dimensions: ambient temperatures, cooling set-points, IT demand) and energy metrics ( c opt c_{\mathrm{opt}} , 10 dimensions: total power, carbon intensity, etc.). At inference, D2C optimizes the 10 energy metric targets to minimize emissions. The objective is to minimize operational carbon emissions while satisfying a hard workload conservation constraint: the total compute delivered must equal the demand (the integral of the optimized profile must match the reference within a tight tolerance). Additional constraints include inlet temperature safety limits. Final designs are validated against the full SustainDC thermal model (Appendix C ). 4.2 Design-Bench Benchmarks To position D2C among established MBO methods, we evaluate on four tasks from Design-Bench [ 30 ] : Ant Morphology (continuous, 60-d), D’Kitty Morphology (continuous, 56-d), TF Bind 8 (discrete, 8-d), and TF Bind 10 (discrete, 10-d). These tasks span transcription factor binding (DNA sequence design) and robot morphology optimization, providing a diverse testbed for offline optimization from fixed datasets. Existing approaches include forward methods that optimize a learned surrogate in design space [ 31 , 9 , 36 , 37 , 4 ] , inverse methods that map target scores to designs with increasingly expressive generators [ 2 , 7 , 19 , 16 , 18 ] , and trajectory-based methods that learn to improve from synthetic optimization paths [ 23 , 3 , 39 ] . Forward methods remain limited by surrogate extrapolation, while inverse and trajectory-based methods typically keep the conditioning target fixed at inference time rather than refining it against downstream objectives. Recent diffusion-based optimization methods attempt to integrate optimization feedback into generation, including guided warm-starts with Langevin corrections [ 17 ] , uncertainty-aware conditioning selection [ 35 ] , editing-based optimization against pseudo-targets [ 38 ] , and end-to-end gradient propagation through diffusion samplers in image-generation settings [ 33 , 27 ] . However, these methods either operate outside offline MBO, rely on post-hoc corrections or heuristic target selection, or do not study physics-informed constrained design with a frozen proposer-evaluator architecture.
